topic: Science grew from practical knowledge in ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, China and Mesoamerica: astronomy for calendars, mathematics for building and trade, and medicine.
Greek natural philosophers sought general explanations; their work was preserved and extended in the medieval Islamic world and Byzantium, and returned to Europe in the 12th century.
The Scientific Revolution of the 16th–17th centuries made experiment and mathematical law the method of natural science.
From the 19th century science became a profession, splitting into disciplines that produced evolution, germ theory, atomic and quantum physics, genetics and the Big Bang.

Approaches to history of science: Historians debate what counts as 'science' before the modern word existed, and whether its history is one of steady progress.
Thomas Kuhn's idea of 'paradigm shifts' (1962) and later sociological studies changed how the history of science is written.
Prehistory: Before writing, knowledge of plants, animals, tools and seasons was passed down orally.
Practical knowledge was mixed with magic, divination and ritual.
Ancient Near East and North East Africa: Mesopotamia and Egypt (about 3000–1200 BC) produced the earliest written mathematics, astronomy and medicine.
Babylonians used a base-60 number system and recorded and predicted planetary motions.
Egyptian mathematics and medicine were practical: land survey, building and medical texts.
Ancient and medieval South Asia and East: Indian mathematicians (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Bhāskara II) developed the decimal place-value system and zero; Pāṇini wrote a formal grammar of Sanskrit.
Chinese astronomers kept long records of eclipses, comets and supernovae; China invented paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass.
Both traditions had sophisticated medicine and logic.
Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica: The Zapotec and Maya developed writing and complex calendars.
Maya astronomers predicted the movements of Venus and eclipses and used a place-value number system with a zero.
Mesoamerican peoples also achieved notable engineering, architecture and Aztec medicine.
Classical antiquity and Greco-Roman natu: Greek thinkers from Thales and Pythagoras on sought natural explanations; Democritus proposed atoms and Hippocrates founded rational medicine.
Plato and Aristotle built systematic philosophies; Euclid organised geometry into proofs.
In the Hellenistic period Archimedes, Hipparchus and the scholars of Alexandria made major advances in mechanics and astronomy.
Middle Ages: After Rome's fall in the West, Greek learning survived in Byzantium and was translated and extended in the Islamic Golden Age.
Al-Khwarizmi founded algebra, Ibn al-Haytham transformed optics, and Avicenna and Averroes wrote influential works on medicine and Aristotle.
Translations from Arabic sparked the Renaissance of the 12th century in Europe and the scholastic universities.
Renaissance: Printing spread texts quickly; scholars recovered Greek originals such as Ptolemy's 'Geography'.
Copernicus's sun-centred system (1543) and Vesalius's anatomy (1543) challenged ancient authorities.
Scientific Revolution and birth of New S: Kepler, Galileo, Descartes and Pascal replaced Aristotle's physics with mathematics and experiment.
Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation (1687) became the model of a scientific theory; Newton and Leibniz invented calculus.
Scientific societies and journals were founded; Enlightenment thinkers such as Voltaire and Kant spread the scientific outlook, and Lavoisier founded modern chemistry.
Romanticism and Post-Scientific Revoluti: Experiments on electricity culminated in Volta's battery (1800).
Adam Smith's 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776) applied systematic analysis to economics.
19th century: Science became a profession; William Whewell coined the word 'scientist' in 1833.
Dalton's atomic theory, Faraday's electromagnetism, Darwin's evolution by natural selection and Mendel's laws of inheritance transformed their fields.
Pasteur's germ theory of disease and vaccines revolutionised medicine.
20th century: Relativity and quantum mechanics (Planck, Einstein, Bohr) rebuilt physics; astronomers discovered the expanding universe and the Big Bang.
Crick and Watson's DNA double helix (1953) founded molecular biology, leading to the Human Genome Project; plate tectonics transformed geology.
Science became 'big science', with huge state-funded projects in particle physics, space and computing.
21st century: The Higgs boson was found in 2012 and gravitational waves detected in 2015.
Genomics, neuroscience and climate science are among the fastest-growing fields.
